O dativo é o caso do “a quem” e “para qu: The dative is the "to whom / for whom" case. In English it hides in word order ("I give him the book") or behind "to" ("I give the book to him"). But there are three traps where English uses a plain object and German needs the dative.
I give the man the book.
PASSO 1: o DATIVO responde a «wem?» (a q: STEP 1: the DATIVE answers «wem?» (to whom?). It marks the person who RECEIVES, hears or benefits from the action — the INDIRECT OBJECT: in «Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel», what I give is «einen Apfel» (accusative, the direct object), and who receives it is «dem Kind» (dative). STEP 2: definite articles in the dative: masculine «dem», feminine «der», neuter «dem», plural «den». STEP 3: indefinite articles: masculine «einem», feminine «einer», neuter «einem»; the plural has no «ein» (with «kein»: «keinen»). STEP 4: in the PLURAL, the noun adds «-n»: «den Kindern», «den Freunden» (except nouns already ending in -n or -s: «den Eltern», «den Autos»). STEP 5: trick: masculine and neuter are IDENTICAL in the dative (dem, einem) — the -m is the same one you see in English "him" and "whom". STEP 6: compare the three columns in the table and read them out loud, column by column.
em português o objeto indireto vem com «: English marks the indirect object with "to" or with word order ("give the apple to the boy" / "give the boy the apple"). German drops the "to" and changes the article: «dem Kind». Your English ear already knows the ending: him, whom, them — dative -m.
I give the book to the man.
I send the woman a letter.
I give the child a toy.
I show the photo to the children.
The receiver goes into the dative: «dem».

PASSO 1: os pronomes pessoais também têm: STEP 1: personal pronouns have a dative form too: mir (to me), dir (to you), ihm (to him, to it), ihr (to her), uns (to us), euch (to you all), ihnen (to them), Ihnen (to you, formal). STEP 2: they replace «dem Mann», «der Frau», «den Kindern» so you don't repeat the noun: «Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch» → «Ich gebe ihm das Buch» (I give him the book). STEP 3: compare the three columns of the table: nominative («ich»), accusative («mich») and dative («mir»). English "me" covers both «mich» and «mir» — German doesn't. Careful: «uns» and «euch» are the same in the accusative and the dative. STEP 4: these verbs usually take TWO objects (dative + accusative), just like English "give someone something": geben, schenken, schicken, zeigen, erzählen, leihen, anbieten, empfehlen. STEP 5: «wünschen» is a classic: «Ich wünsche dir einen schönen Tag» (I wish you a nice day).

PASSO 1: se a frase tem DOIS SUBSTANTIVO: STEP 1: if the sentence has TWO NOUNS, the dative comes first: «Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball» (like "I give the child the ball"). STEP 2: if one of them is a PRONOUN, the pronoun comes first: «Ich gebe ihm den Ball» (dative pronoun + accusative noun) and «Ich gebe ihn dem Kind» (accusative pronoun + dative noun — "I give it to the child"). STEP 3: if BOTH are pronouns, the ACCUSATIVE comes first: «Ich gebe ihn ihm» ("I give it to him"). STEP 4: remember the dative plural with «-n»: «den Kindern».

Helfen rege dativo. No plural, o artigo: «Helfen» takes the dative. In the plural, the article is «den» and «Kinder» adds -n: Ich helfe den Kindern.
Helfen rege dativo. O pronome du passa a: «Helfen» takes the dative. The pronoun «du» becomes «dir», not «dich»: Ich helfe dir.
Gehören indica aqui a quem o livro perte: «Gehören» says who the book belongs to, and it takes the dative. «Ich» becomes «mir»: Das Buch gehört mir.
